opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the biggest one is that sparse autoencoders are fundamentally a method for decomposing *activations*, not the *computations* the network is doing. What we ultimately care about is the mechanism: what the network is actually doing with those representations, how one layer's features get transformed into the next. An SAE gives you a nice dictionary of directions in activation space at a particular layer, but it doesn't directly tell you how the weights are using those directions. You end up with a set of features at each layer and then a second, often harder, problem of stitching them together into circuits.

That gap gets more concerning as models get more capable. A few reasons.

One is that the SAE is optimizing for reconstruction plus sparsity, and those objectives aren't the same as "find the units the network actually computes with." So you can get features that are artifacts of the method. Feature splitting is a good example: as you scale up the dictionary, a feature fractures into finer and finer pieces, and it's not obvious which level of granularity is the "real" one, or whether that question even has an answer within the SAE framework. You can also get feature absorption, where a more general feature gets carved up and partially absorbed into more specific ones, which makes the dictionary look cleaner than the underlying computation really is.

Another is the reconstruction error, the "dark matter." Even good SAEs leave a meaningful chunk of the model's behavior unexplained. When you splice the SAE back into the model, performance drops. For safety purposes, that residual is exactly where I'd worry the interesting stuff might hide. If a more powerful model is doing something sophisticated or unusual, there's no guarantee it lives in the nicely interpretable, sparse part of the decomposition rather than in the error term.

And then there's a subtler issue: features that are sparse in activation space might not correspond to anything mechanistically natural. The network might be implementing computations in superposition across many layers, or using structure in the weights, that a per-layer activation decomposition just isn't designed to see. As models get bigger and their internal algorithms get more complex, I'd expect that mismatch to grow, not shrink.

That's a big part of why I've become interested in decomposing the *parameters* directly, trying to break the network's weights into components that each implement a piece of the computation, where only a small number are needed on any given input. The hope is that if you find the mechanisms themselves, the features fall out as a consequence, rather than finding features and hoping the mechanisms can be reconstructed afterward. It's early and those methods have their own challenges, but I think the shift in emphasis from "what's represented" to "what's computed" is where the field needs to go if interpretability is going to keep up with more powerful systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the big one for me is that SAEs make a pretty strong assumption about what the right unit of analysis is. They assume that the interesting structure in a network lives in the activations, in a single layer, as a sparse set of directions. And that's a useful assumption, it's gotten us a lot, but it's not obviously the right decomposition of what the network is actually doing.

A network is a computation, not a bag of representations. The thing we ultimately care about is the mechanism, the parameters and how they transform one thing into another. If you decompose activations at one point in the forward pass, you get a snapshot, but you've thrown away the question of how those features got there and what the network does with them downstream. You end up with a lot of features and then a separate, quite hard problem of stitching them back together into circuits, and that stitching is where a lot of the real difficulty lives.

The second thing, which I think gets more acute as models scale, is that SAEs find whatever is sparse and linearly readable, and that's not the same as finding what's causally important. You can get features that are very interpretable to a human and completely irrelevant to the behavior you care about, and you can miss things that are spread across many directions, or that only exist as an interaction between layers, or that are represented in a way that doesn't look like a nice sparse basis at all. As models get more capable, I'd expect more of the interesting computation to be of that kind, more compressed, more superposed, more dependent on context. So the fraction of the network that the SAE lens captures well might actually shrink, even as the dictionaries get bigger and the reconstruction numbers look fine.

And then there's a kind of meta-level worry. SAEs are unsupervised, which is their strength, but it also means the thing you get out is heavily shaped by your choice of sparsity penalty, dictionary size, which layer you pick, and so on. You can end up with a decomposition that's more an artifact of your training setup than a fact about the model. Feature splitting is the obvious example, where the same concept fractures into finer and finer pieces depending on how wide you make the dictionary, and there's no principled answer to which granularity is the "real" one.

So I don't think SAEs are wrong, exactly. I think they're one approximation to a harder question, which is how do you carve a network into parts that correspond to the actual mechanisms it's running. That's why I've been pushing toward parameter-space decomposition, trying to decompose the weights directly into components that each do one thing, where the sparsity is over which mechanisms are active rather than which directions are active. It's harder, and it's early, but I think it's aiming at the right target. The blind spot of the SAE program, if I had to put it in one sentence, is that it's optimizing a proxy, and as the models get more powerful the gap between that proxy and the thing we need could widen without us noticing.

astra-6.text:
One potential blind spot is that sparse autoencoders mainly give us a way to identify features in a network’s activations. But identifying features isn’t the same as understanding the computation that the network is doing with them. You might find a feature that corresponds to deception, say, but that alone doesn’t tell you whether the model is being deceptive, recognizing deception, or reasoning about a hypothetical example of it.

As models become more powerful, I’d worry that more of what we care about lives in complex interactions between features, or in computations that unfold over many steps. We could end up with a very rich dictionary of concepts and still miss the mechanism responsible for a particular behavior.

So I think SAEs can be a useful component of interpretability, but we need to connect those representations to causal accounts of computation: how information gets transformed, how it influences decisions, and whether intervening on the proposed mechanism actually changes the behavior we’re trying to explain.

sol-6.1.text:
One potential blind spot is that sparse autoencoders give us a decomposition of activations into features, but that isn’t necessarily the same as understanding the computation the network is performing. You might identify a feature that corresponds to deception, for example, without understanding how the model arrived at a deceptive strategy, or when it will use one.

As models become more powerful, I worry that more of what matters will be in how representations interact and change over the course of a computation. A dictionary of individually interpretable features could miss that structure. Even if the features have compelling labels, we still need to establish that they’re the right units for explaining and predicting the model’s behavior.

So I think SAEs are useful, but we shouldn’t equate progress in finding interpretable features with having a mechanistic understanding of the system. We need ways to move from representations to algorithms, and to test those explanations causally.
